title: Affordability or Antifascism Is a False Choice
text:
Supported by
Guest Essay
Americans Are Worried About More Than Prices
As we process the Democratic Party’s midterm victory, a widely agreed-upon narrative is emerging: This was an affordability election. From South Carolina to Ohio to California, voters rallied behind Democratic candidates who spoke to kitchen-table concerns.
But it would be wrong, and ultimately dangerous, to interpret voters’ preference for Democrats exclusively as a reaction to rising prices.
This election was also a profoundly antifascist one.
Americans desperately want and need costs to come down, and delivering on that should be the Democratic Party’s first priority. But the landslide that redrew political maps, particularly in the South, cannot be explained solely by anger at grocery and gasoline prices. It was also powered by a deep sense of moral revulsion and indignation that has only gained force since 2024.
The tone of these midterms was set by ordinary people who stuck their necks out by bravely opposing Elon Musk, immigration enforcement, data centers and the carnage in Gaza well before those positions were safely mainstream.
Let’s remember how, in the early days of the second Trump administration, an atmosphere of fear descended over the nation as many elite institutions — universities, law firms, media outlets and tech companies — bent the knee, convinced that a permanent proto-fascist “vibe shift” had arrived. Thankfully, not everyone was so eager to acquiesce.
Soon after the inauguration, Tesla Takedown protests popped up at Tesla dealerships and spread widely, much to the irritation of Elon Musk, who was then gleefully beginning to gut the federal work force. People kept showing up even after President Trump threatened to classify those who vandalized Tesla cars as “domestic terrorists” and send them to Salvadoran prisons.
